previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex history of sclerosing mesenteritis, chronic partial small bowel obstruction, and gastrostomy dependence was admitted for increased abdominal pain and bilious vomiting. Imaging showed slightly worsened dilation of proximal small bowel loops, consistent with her chronic condition. She was managed conservatively with bowel rest, IV fluids, and her established pain protocol using IV Dilaudid and Phenergan. Surgery recommended no intervention. She tolerated a trial of oral intake, her symptoms improved, and she was discharged home in stable condition. All home medications were continued without changes, and she was advised to follow up regarding her G-tube size. TPN was resumed at discharge.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ with a long history of sclerosing mesenteritis s/p 23 
abdominal surgeries who presents with recurrent abdominal pain 
and subjective orthostasis.  
.  
# Orthostasis:  The patient reported subjective orthostasis 
without pre-syncopal signs.  She had no nausea, vomiting, 
diaphoresis, or sensation of falling.  There was no sign of 
infection clinically or per testing (UA, CXR).  Orthostatic 
vital signs were not impressive, with borderline elevation of HR 
and no substantive change in BP.  DDx dehydration, medication 
effect, and anxiety.  She received hydration with good effect 
but no change in her subjective symptoms.  Although she 
experienced these symptoms at home when she does not have access 
to IV Dilaudid, she received this medication approximately 
weekly and may have a delayed release or withdrawl effect.  In 
addition, clonidine and Abilify both have the potential to cause 
orthostasis and tachycardia.  The doses of both medications were 
recently increased.  
.
It is likely that she will experience orthostasis at some times 
given her extensive medication list.  We were hesitant to alter 
any aspect of her medication regimen given the complexity of her 
care.  However, it did seem likely that the increased dose of 
one or both of these medications is the cause of her recent 
symptoms.  We therefore proposed reducing the dose of Abilify 
back to 2mg daily, her initial dose.  We confirmed this plan 
with the primary care physician.  The patient attempted to 
contact her psychopharmacologist who was not immediately 
available.  We recommended this reduction and continued 
follow-up with her providers.  The patient agreed with this 
plan.  We were, however, reassured that she was not clinically 
presyncopal and did not have empiric orthostatic hypotension.
.
# Abdominal pain:  Chronic issue with complex management.  We 
made no changes to her regimen during her stay.  She continued 
her home TPN infusion.  She received 2.5mg IV Dilaudid in the ED 
according to her pain protocol.
.
